lead: Photodetector noise sets the smallest current a receiver can trust. Shot noise comes from random carrier arrival. Thermal noise comes from the load resistor. Shot noise follows photocurrent plus dark current; thermal noise follows resistance and temperature. Add noise powers, not rms currents. The signal-to-noise ratio tells whether the receiver is shot-limited or thermal-limited. Only a few universities teach this as a stand-alone topic.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for responsivity, Chapter 4.2 for photocurrent, and Chapter 4.3 for APD gain and excess noise factor.

blocks.text: Shot noise comes from random arrival times. A 1 µA photocurrent is about 6 × 10¹² electrons per second, each crossing unpredictably. Carriers obey Poisson statistics because each arrives independently. Shot noise grows with current and bandwidth.

blocks.where: q = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is electron charge; I<sub>ph</sub> is photocurrent in A; I<sub>d</sub> is dark current in A; B is post-detection bandwidth in Hz. For an APD, photocurrent and bulk dark current carry M²F; surface dark current adds directly. M is gain, F is excess noise factor.

blocks.text: Thermal noise is the load resistor's current jitter. It exists with no light; it is set by the resistor and amplifier input. For a PIN, put M = 1 and F = 1 in the shot formula. B is post-detection bandwidth, not optical frequency.

blocks.where: k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K; T is temperature in K; R<sub>L</sub> is load resistance in Ω.

sections.h3: Adding noise and the signal-to-noise ratio

blocks.text: Noise currents are independent, so powers add: σ² = ish2 + ith2. Here σ² is total mean-square noise current in A²; σ is rms in A. Add powers, not rms currents: 5.06 nA and 40.7 nA give about 41 nA because 40.7² dominates.

blocks.where: I<sub>ph</sub> is photocurrent in A; σ² is total mean-square noise current in A².

blocks.text: If thermal noise dominates, SNR ≈ I<sub>ph</sub>²R<sub>L</sub>/(4kTB). Since I<sub>ph</sub> ∝ P, SNR rises as P², or 20 dB per decade. If shot noise dominates, SNR ≈ I<sub>ph</sub>/(2qB), so it rises as P, or 10 dB per decade.

Dark current has a bulk part, proportional to depleted volume, and a surface leakage part. Only the bulk part is multiplied by M in an APD; the surface part adds directly. Write I<sub>d</sub> = M·I<sub>db</sub> + I<sub>ds</sub>, with I<sub>db</sub> the bulk part in A, I<sub>ds</sub> the surface part in A, and M the gain. Low-frequency 1/f noise appears below a few kHz and is small in a good diode. A larger R<sub>L</sub> lowers thermal noise but raises the R<sub>L</sub>C time constant, so bandwidth falls.

blocks.where: σ<sub>rms</sub> is rms noise current per unit bandwidth in A/√Hz; R is responsivity in A/W; NEP is in W/√Hz, the optical power giving SNR = 1 in a 1 Hz bandwidth.

figure.caption: Random diode current produces shot noise and the load resistor produces thermal noise; the two mean-square currents add before the signal-to-noise ratio is taken.

spec.title: Noise sources at the photodiode
spec.aria: Two noise branches, shot noise from the diode current and thermal noise from the load resistor, joining into a total noise block that gives the output signal-to-noise ratio.

examples.question: A PIN receiver has responsivity R = 0.8 A/W, received optical power P = 1 µW, dark current I<sub>d</sub> = 1 nA, post-detection bandwidth B = 100 MHz, load R<sub>L</sub> = 1 kΩ at T = 300 K. Find the shot-noise rms current, thermal-noise rms current, total rms noise, SNR and SNR in dB.
steps: I<sub>ph</sub> = RP = 0.8 × 10⁻⁶ = 8.00 × 10⁻⁷ A; I<sub>ph</sub> + I<sub>d</sub> = 8.01 × 10⁻⁷ A.
examples.answer: Shot noise 5.06 nA rms, thermal 40.7 nA rms, total 41.0 nA rms, SNR 381 or 25.8 dB. The receiver is thermal-noise limited.
examples.check:
import math
q=1.6e-19
k=1.38e-23
R=0.8
P=1e-6
Id=1e-9
B=1e8
RL=1000.0
T=300.0
Iph=R*P
I=Iph+Id
shot=2*q*I*B
th=4*k*T*B/RL
tot=shot+th
snr=Iph**2/tot
print(f'{shot**0.5:.3g}')
print(f'{th**0.5:.3g}')
print(f'{tot**0.5:.3g}')
print(f'{snr:.3g}')
print(f'{10*math.log10(snr):.3g}')

traps: Adding rms noise currents. Add mean-square powers, then take one square root.
Using I<sub>ph</sub> in shot noise and forgetting I<sub>d</sub>.
For an APD, putting M or M²F in the wrong place. Signal current is M I<sub>ph</sub>; shot-noise power carries M²F for photocurrent and bulk dark current only.
Treating a bigger R<sub>L</sub> as free. It lowers thermal noise but raises R<sub>L</sub>C and narrows B.
Quoting SNR in dB as 20 log₁₀ instead of 10 log₁₀ of a power ratio.

quiz.q: Write the PIN shot-noise mean-square formula and define every symbol.
quiz.a: ish² = 2q(Iph + Id)B; q is electron charge, Iph photocurrent, Id dark current, B post-detection bandwidth.

quiz.q: Why add noise powers rather than rms currents?
quiz.a: Independent random currents have variances that add. Total rms is √(i_sh² + i_th²), not i_sh + i_th.

quiz.q: A PIN has R = 1.0 A/W, P = 2 µW, I<sub>d</sub> = 0, B = 50 MHz, R<sub>L</sub> = 2 kΩ, T = 300 K. Which noise term dominates? Give both mean-square values.
quiz.a: Shot = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ A²; thermal = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁶ A². Thermal noise dominates.

quiz.q: Explain why SNR rises 20 dB per decade under the thermal limit and 10 dB per decade under the shot limit.
quiz.a: Thermal-limited SNR ∝ I<sub>ph</sub>² ∝ P², so 20 dB per decade. Shot-limited SNR ∝ I<sub>ph</sub> ∝ P, so 10 dB per decade.

quiz.q: An APD has M = 10, F = 5, primary current I = 1 µA, B = 100 MHz. Find the shot mean-square current using q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Define NEP and give its unit.
quiz.a: NEP = σ<sub>rms</sub>/R is the optical power giving SNR = 1 in a 1 Hz bandwidth; unit W/√Hz. σ<sub>rms</sub> is noise current per unit bandwidth in A/√Hz.

quiz.q: Name the two parts of dark current and say how APD gain affects them.
quiz.a: Bulk current proportional to depleted volume, and surface leakage. In an APD only the bulk part is multiplied by M: I<sub>d</sub> = M·I<sub>db</sub> + I<sub>ds</sub>. Surface leakage adds directly.

beyond: Not for exam. Coherent and balanced detection can cancel local-oscillator noise and reach shot-noise-limited performance. Transimpedance amplifiers trade resistor noise against bandwidth and input capacitance. Search 'noise equivalent power photodiode', 'transimpedance amplifier input-referred noise', and 'shot-noise-limited optical receiver'.
